subject: Automotive & EVs
title: Cars as Computers on Wheels
description: A quick win: understand Cars as Computers on Wheels.

hook.text: A modern car has more lines of code than a fighter jet. Software defines the driving experience.

buildup.text: Touchscreens replaced buttons. Over-the-air updates change your car while it sits in the garage.

discovery.text: Tesla proved that a car's features could improve after purchase—just like a phone getting new apps.

twist.text: But it also means subscription fees for heated seats and features locked behind paywalls.

climax.text: The auto industry is shifting from selling hardware to selling software and recurring revenue.

punchline.text: You used to own your car. Now it gets updates.

quiz.question: What do over-the-air updates allow?
options: Updating car software without a shop visit

details.summary: Modern cars contain over 100 microprocessors managing everything from engine timing to infotainment, transforming vehicles from purely mechanical machines into rolling computer networks.
details.whyItMatters: The shift to software-controlled systems enabled safety features like stability control and ABS, but also introduced cybersecurity risks and software complexity unprecedented in automotive history.
takeaways: A modern car can have over 100 million lines of code
Electronic control units manage braking, steering, and throttle
Software updates now rival engine changes in importance

faq.question: When did cars start relying heavily on computers?
faq.answer: The transition accelerated in the 1980s with electronic fuel injection and gained momentum through the 1990s and 2000s as regulations required more precise emissions and safety systems.

faq.question: Can car computers be hacked?
faq.answer: Security researchers have demonstrated remote exploits on connected vehicles, prompting automakers to invest heavily in automotive cybersecurity and adopt secure software development practices.
